name: dragonbox
desc: Reference implementation of Dragonbox in C++
why: Reference implementation of an elegant shortest float-to-string algorithm, a close call showing how numbers become text.

brief.what_it_is: Dragonbox is a C++ library that converts a floating-point number into the shortest decimal digits that will read back as the same number. Given a nonzero finite float or double, its to_decimal function returns a decimal significand, a decimal exponent, and optionally a sign flag. A separate to_chars function, shipped with the library, turns those integers into a text string such as 1.234E0 for the input 1.234. The core dragonbox.h header is header-only. The string-generation part adds dragonbox_to_chars.h and dragonbox_to_chars.cpp. The package is not a command-line tool and has no executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a successor to Schubfach, a float-to-string algorithm by Raffaello Giulietti, and as inspired by Grisu and Grisu-Exact. It promises three things: round-trip correctness, the shortest output length, and correct rounding among the shortest candidates. The name comes from the pigeonhole principle, which Schubfach calls the drawer principle and which is also known as Dirichlet's box principle. Dragonbox keeps the box idea and adds Grisu's dragon.
brief.how_it_works: Dragonbox does not produce the final string. It computes the decimal significand and exponent that a string generator then formats, and the README says the string step is not officially part of the algorithm. The README says the algorithm is explained in a paper at other_files/Dragonbox.pdf, which includes a mathematical proof. It also says the proof was checked with verification programs in the test and meta directories. The README does not describe the internal arithmetic in more detail.

brief.install_notes: Not a Homebrew-style CLI. The library is C++11 or later, and every function is constexpr since C++20. Header-only use needs only dragonbox.h. For string output, add dragonbox_to_chars.h and dragonbox_to_chars.cpp. Setup can be manual, or done through CMake with FetchContent_Declare and FetchContent_MakeAvailable, then target_link_libraries against dragonbox::dragonbox or dragonbox::dragonbox_to_chars. A system install can use find_package(dragonbox). The benchmark subproject runs MATLAB scripts and must have its working directory set to subproject/benchmark. Non-Visual Studio generators need that set by hand.
brief.standout: The output is guaranteed to be the shortest, correctly rounded string that round-trips, and the README presents this as a tie-break-aware refinement of Schubfach. The policy system is also unusual: sign handling, trailing-zero handling, rounding mode for parsing and for formatting, and the cache size are all compile-time choices. The README also says the fmt library uses an almost identical implementation.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no release version or last-commit date. Its benchmarks are dated 03/30/2024, which is the only date evidence. I did not check the commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: to_decimal is only defined for finite nonzero inputs. Behavior with infinities, NaN, or zeros is undefined, although to_chars and to_chars_n accept any input. Each policy combination creates a separate template instantiation, which can bloat binaries. The compact cache is about 20 percent slower, and the README says it has no effect on float. The README says the Schubfach comparison is not completely fair. The Clang and MSVC benchmark images are not described in text. Licensing is dual Apache 2.0 with LLVM exceptions or Boost 1.0, with third-party code in subproject/3rdparty excluded. The main implementation is described as hard to read, and the README points to a simpler version in subproject/simple for porting.
quotes: Dragonbox is a float-to-string conversion algorithm based on a beautiful algorithm Schubfach, developed by Raffaello Giulietti in 2017-2018.
Since there are only three files, it should be not difficult to set up this library manually if you want, but you can also use it via CMake as explained below.

judge.reason: Dragonbox makes an invisible everyday operation—the correctly rounded, shortest float-to-decimal conversion—into a compact, mathematically proved algorithm you can inspect.

entry.title: Dragonbox
entry.tldr: A C++ library that finds the shortest decimal string a float will read back as exactly, with a published proof of why it works.
entry.deeper_look:
Dragonbox converts a nonzero finite float or double into a decimal significand and exponent. The digits are the shortest ones that still round-trip to the same number. Among the shortest candidates, it picks the correctly rounded one. A companion `to_chars` function turns those integers into text, so 1.234 comes out as `1.234E0`.

It exists because printing floats is harder than it looks. The number you typed, 0.3, is not the number stored in the machine. Printing the stored value naively gives a long tail of digits, and printing too few digits gives back a different number. Dragonbox is the author's successor to Schubfach by Raffaello Giulietti, and it is inspired by Grisu and Grisu-Exact. The name nods to the pigeonhole principle, which Schubfach calls the drawer principle and which is also known as Dirichlet's box principle. Dragonbox keeps the box and adds Grisu's dragon.

The repository is a good door into how numbers become text. The README points to a paper, `other_files/Dragonbox.pdf`, that explains the algorithm and includes a mathematical proof. It says the proof was checked with verification programs in the test and meta directories. The main implementation is, in the author's words, "riddled with template indirections obscuring the core logic of the algorithm." For reading, the README points to a simpler version in `subproject/simple`.

The string step is not officially part of the algorithm. The README says the fmt library uses an almost identical implementation.

brew install dragonbox
